definition.text: The presence in soil of human-made chemicals or other changes to the natural soil environment, a form of land degradation; also called soil or land pollution.

facts.text: It usually comes from industry, farm chemicals or poor waste disposal; the commonest chemicals are petroleum hydrocarbons, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides and heavy metals.
The main worry is health: people meet contaminants by touching soil, eating plants grown in it, breathing its vapours, or drinking groundwater polluted from below.
At low levels contamination is often within a soil's own capacity to treat waste: soil organisms transform it, mainly through microbial enzymes, and organic matter and clay adsorb it.
Overloading that capacity harms soil life and soil function; derelict soils are damaged so badly by industrial contamination or development that the land cannot be used safely or productively.
Mapping contaminated sites and cleaning them up is slow and costly, calling on geology, hydrology, chemistry, computer modelling and GIS, and on the site's pollution history.
Its extent is best known in North America and Europe, where many countries have legal frameworks for finding and dealing with contaminated land; elsewhere regulation tends to be looser.
In 2012 EU member states reported over 2.5 million potentially contaminated sites and about 342 thousand identified ones; mineral oil and heavy metals made up around 60% of the contamination.
Sampling found about 100,000 square kilometres of China's cultivated land polluted; with land irrigated by contaminated water or buried by solid waste, that is one-tenth of its cultivable land.

definition.text: The activities and materials that put contaminants into soil, such as mining and heavy industry, spills, leaking underground storage tanks, agrochemicals and waste disposal.

facts.text: Listed causes also include microplastics, oil spills and fuel dumping, construction, lead-based exterior paint, nuclear waste, sewage discharge, landfills and illegal dumping, and electronic waste.
Road traffic adds lead from vehicle exhaust and cadmium and zinc from tyre wear, and some rocks are naturally rich in toxic elements.
Ash from coal burned for heating and for ore smelting was a common source of contamination in areas industrialized before about 1960.
Coal concentrates arsenic, cadmium, lead and zinc as it forms; burning leaves most of these metals in the ash, except mercury, which evaporates.
Coal ash also carries polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, known human carcinogens whose acceptable soil concentrations typically range from 0.1 mg/kg to 10 mg/kg depending on the compound.
Treated sewage sludge (biosolids) is a controversial fertilizer: rich in nitrogen, phosphate and potassium, but generally carrying more organisms, pesticides and heavy metals than other soil.
Composting sludge cuts its pathogens and most organic pollutants, though not persistent organic pollutants, and leaves its heavy metals in place, if in a less bioavailable form.
Repeated fungicide sprays build up copper in vineyards and orchards, even on organic farms, an example of diffuse contamination.

title: Microplastics in soil

definition.text: Insoluble synthetic plastic particles between 1 micrometre and 5 millimetres across, which pollute soil as well as water and air.

facts.text: Primary microplastics, such as clothing microfibres and pellets, are already small when released; secondary ones form as larger plastic items weather and break down in the environment.
Every agricultural soil sample tested from southwestern China held plastic particles, 92% of them microfibres, probably from string, twine and irrigation water used to wash clothes.
Spreading biosolids from sewage sludge and compost adds microplastics to soil, on top of inputs from other sources such as the atmosphere.
About half the sewage sludge in Europe and North America goes onto farmland; in Europe 113 to 770 tonnes of microplastics per million inhabitants are estimated to reach farm soils each year.
Soil animals such as earthworms, mites and springtails may grind swallowed plastic debris into smaller microplastics as it passes through their guts.
A 2024 meta-analysis of 180 studies found microplastics raised soil carbon dioxide emissions by 25.7% and soil organic carbon by 25.4%, and cut aboveground plant biomass.
Plastic mulch film residues affect wheat growth, and microplastics can change plant roots, leaves and biomass, with effects depending strongly on the type of plastic.
Much microplastic is expected to end up in soils, yet most studies only report its presence, not its origin or quantity.

title: Pesticides in soil

definition.text: Chemical or biological agents used to kill pests such as weeds, insects and fungi, and a major class of soil contaminant.

facts.text: Pesticides include herbicides, insecticides, nematicides and fungicides; herbicides are the most common, at about 50% of all pesticide use worldwide.
Over 98% of sprayed insecticides and 95% of herbicides end up somewhere other than their target, including air, water and soil.
Most herbicides are broken down by soil bacteria, but 2,4-D and 2,4,5-T can carry the impurity dioxin, which is lethal even at low concentrations.
Paraquat, banned in the EU, is highly toxic and breaks down slowly in soil because it is adsorbed and protected within clay lattices.
Soil bacteria quickly turn glyphosate into AMPA, yet glyphosate residues are still detected in drinking water, farm produce and food.

Synthetic insecticides form three main groups: persistent organochlorines such as DDT, organophosphates that block nerve transmission, and neonicotinoids that act on the insect central nervous system.
Neonicotinoids degrade in soil, but large-scale use has greatly increased their residues, and they harm beneficial insects such as pollinators as well as pests.
Adsorption to soil can slow a pesticide's movement but also hide it from microbes that would degrade it; halogens in a molecule often slow its aerobic breakdown.

title: DDT

definition.text: A cheap, potent and persistent organochlorine insecticide, used on a massive scale from the 1930s.

facts.text: Use peaked at 72,000 tonnes in 1970 and then fell as its harm became clear; it turned up worldwide in fish and birds and even in Antarctic snow.
Barely soluble in water but very soluble in fats, it thins birds' eggshells and is blamed for the 1950s decline of ospreys and peregrine falcons, now recovering.
Its half-life in soil is 2–15 years, so residues are still found in people, at levels 5 to 10 times lower than in the 1970s.
The Stockholm Convention banned it in 2001; in 2006 the World Health Organization allowed it back only for controlling vector-borne diseases in some tropical countries.
A persistent organic pollutant, DDT sorbs readily to soils and sediments, which act both as sinks and as long-term sources of exposure for organisms.
It leaves soil through runoff, volatilization and photolysis and is broken down by aerobic and anaerobic microbes; its breakdown products DDE and DDD are just as persistent.
Long after the bans, a 2018 study still found DDT residues in European soils and Spanish rivers.
Global distillation carries DDT and its breakdown products from warm regions to the Arctic, where they build up in the food web.

conflicts.text: Depending on environmental conditions, its soil half-life can range from 22 days to 30 years.
conflicts.note: The Pesticide page gives a soil half-life of 2–15 years (c738aae75e75).

definition.text: Soil contamination left by munitions, chemical agents and other agents of war.

facts.text: Disposal of munitions, and careless manufacture under wartime urgency, can contaminate soil for long periods.
Little is published on it, largely because governments restrict publication of material related to the war effort.
Mustard gas stored in World War II contaminated some sites for up to 50 years, and anthrax weapon tests left Gruinard island quarantined for 48 years.
Abandoned munition-dismantling sites along the former World War I front in Belgium and France are still contaminated with arsenic and lead.

definition.text: The routes by which soil contaminants reach people: swallowing soil or dust, eating food grown in it, skin contact, and breathing its vapours or dust.

facts.text: Most exposure is accidental, and some studies estimate that 90% of human exposure comes from eating contaminated food.
A potentially greater threat is contaminants seeping into aquifers used for irrigation or drinking, sometimes far from any visible source: long-range diffuse soil contamination.
Toxic metals climb the food chain through plants growing in metal-rich soils, which tends to lead to pollution-related diseases.
Organic matter and clay can adsorb contaminants, but as suspended colloids they may also carry them down into subsurface environments.
German soil protection law sets test values per pathway: soil to groundwater, soil to crops (stored in tubers or leaves) and soil to humans by dust, skin or children eating soil.

definition.text: The harm that exposure to soil contaminants does to people, which varies with the pollutant, the route of exposure and how vulnerable the exposed people are.

facts.text: Long exposure to chromium, lead and other metals, petroleum, solvents and many pesticides can cause cancer, birth defects or other chronic disease.
Benzene at sufficient concentrations is linked to leukaemia, mercury and cyclodienes to kidney damage, and PCBs and cyclodienes to liver toxicity.
Concentrations of nitrate and ammonia from livestock manure are also health hazards in soil and groundwater.
At high enough doses many soil contaminants can kill through contact, inhalation or ingestion.

definition.text: The damage soil contaminants do to ecosystems, beginning with changes to soil chemistry and to the organisms living in the soil.

facts.text: Many hazardous chemicals change soil chemistry radically even at low concentrations, altering the metabolism of soil microbes and animals.
Wiping out part of the base of the food chain can have major consequences for predators and other consumers.
Earthworms and other soil ecosystem engineers are very sensitive to contaminants; as they decline, the humus form shifts from mull with good crumb structure to undecayed mor over compact soil.
Because humus forms respond this way, a quick look at forest-floor thickness and the mineral horizon below has been proposed as a cheap early check for contamination.
Heavy metals and metalloids on farmland alter plant metabolism and often cut crop yields, and the weakened crops then shield the soil less from erosion.
Some contaminants have long half-lives, and others decay into derivative chemicals that are themselves contaminants.

title: Biomagnification

definition.text: The rise in a substance's concentration in the tissues of organisms at each higher level of a food chain.

facts.text: Persistent, fat-soluble compounds are the classic case: DDT and other organochlorines are stable and lipophilic, so they build up in bodies and food chains.
DDT concentrated in birds that ate contaminated prey weakened their eggshells, raised chick deaths and threatened species with extinction.
PCBs, easily retained in organisms, both build up over an organism's lifetime (bioaccumulation) and magnify up food webs.
Bacteria and archaea turn inorganic mercury into methylmercury, which accumulates in fish such as tuna and swordfish and magnifies further up the food chain.
Bioaccumulation is build-up within one organism from its food and surroundings; biomagnification is the increase across food-chain levels.
Mercury shows the scale: herring hold about 0.01 ppm, sharks more than 1 ppm.
It is measured by the biomagnification factor, the predator-to-prey concentration ratio, and by the trophic magnification factor across a whole food web; values above 1 mean magnification.
Reviews suggest it is rarer than once thought, but DDT, DDE, PCBs, toxaphene and organic mercury and arsenic clearly do biomagnify.

title: Contaminant effects on soil functions
article: Soil contamination#Potential effects of contaminants to soil functions

definition.text: The disruption of soil functions, such as the cycling of carbon and nitrogen, when heavy metals and other contaminants alter the activity, mix and numbers of soil microorganisms.

facts.text: Contaminants can become less bioavailable over time (natural attenuation), and microbes and ecosystems can adapt to the changed conditions.
Soil pH, organic matter content and texture strongly modify how mobile, bioavailable and toxic a pollutant is.
The same amount of a contaminant can be toxic in one soil and harmless in another, so risk assessment and remediation must be soil-specific.

title: Soil remediation

definition.text: Cleaning up contaminated soil by removing, treating or containing its pollutants, to restore the soil's functions and values.

facts.text: Environmental scientists plan cleanups from field measurements of soil chemicals and from computer models, including GIS, of how those chemicals move and change.
Methods are ex situ, excavating soil or pumping groundwater for treatment at the surface, or in situ, treating the contamination without removing soil or water.
The traditional approaches are digging soil out for landfill disposal and 'pump and treat' of groundwater; excavation extends to dredging contaminated bay muds and canals.
Physical options include aerating soil on site, at the risk of air pollution, heating it to volatilize contaminants for vapour extraction, and extracting soil vapour or groundwater for air stripping.
Biological options use microbes (bioremediation), plants such as willow (phytoremediation) or fungi (mycoremediation) to break contaminants down or take up heavy metals.
In situ technologies include solidification and stabilization, soil vapour extraction, permeable reactive barriers, monitored natural attenuation, chemical oxidation and thermal desorption.
Contaminants can instead be contained, behind barrier walls such as slurry walls that must be impermeable and resist attack by the waste for their whole lifespan.
Cleanup may be required before land is redeveloped; it follows regulations or, where no standards exist or they are only advisory, assessments of health and ecological risk.

title: Contaminated land risk assessment

definition.text: The staged evaluation of whether a site's contaminants pose unacceptable risk, moving from a qualitative conceptual site model to generic and then detailed quantitative assessment.

facts.text: Assessment starts once a site is suspected of contamination, often with a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment; the site's past uses guide the sampling and chemical analysis.
A desk study and site walkover feed a conceptual site model; risk needs a 'contaminant linkage' in which a source, a pathway and a receptor are all present.
Site investigation by boreholes or trial pits supplies soil and groundwater samples, judged against the site's proposed end use by generic or detailed assessment.
Neighbouring land is often contaminated too, by decades of emissions or contaminated fill, so nearby topsoil, ceiling dust and water should be tested before and after remediation.
Generic screening values are set conservatively for standard land uses; exceeding one shows only that harm is possible, prompting site-specific study of contaminants, pathways and receptors.
National standards include the US EPA's Preliminary Remediation Goals and Regional Screening Levels, the Dutch standards in Europe, Australia's investigation levels and Canada's provincial standards.
The EU is moving towards Europe-wide standards, though most industrialized European nations still set their own.
Testing is contentious: nobody wants to pay for assessment or cleanup, and findings on nearby land may go on property titles and lower their value.

title: Soil guideline value

definition.text: Figures used in UK non-statutory guidance to help assessors decide whether land counts as contaminated under UK law.

facts.text: They serve the second, generic quantitative stage of risk assessment, as conservative estimates of whether long-term exposure poses unacceptable risk to human health.
The Environment Agency derives them with the CLEA model; anyone can calculate equivalent Generic Assessment Criteria the same way.
They cover three land uses: a residential home whose critical receptor is a girl up to six years old, an allotment, and a commercial office.
They are thresholds for further assessment, not remedial targets.

title: Nonpoint source pollution

definition.text: Diffuse pollution of water or air that does not come from a single, discrete source.

facts.text: It is often the sum of small amounts of contaminants gathered from a large area, unlike point source pollution, which comes from one source.
It comes from land runoff, precipitation, atmospheric deposition, drainage, seepage or hydrological change, which make it hard to trace back to any one source.
Its water pollutants are sediment, nutrients, toxic chemicals and pathogens, from urban areas, farming, the atmosphere, highways, forestry and mining, and marinas.
It stems from the everyday activities of many people, such as fertilizing lawns, spraying pesticides and building, so it is hard to regulate and control.
Nitrogen leaching from fertilized fields and nutrient runoff in sheet flow over fields or forests are typical examples.
A factory smokestack is a point source, but long-range transport and many emitters make its deposition a nonpoint source where it lands.
Urban controls include grass buffer strips that let soil absorb pollutants, retention ponds where contaminants settle, porous pavement and constructed wetlands.
It is the leading cause of water pollution in the United States, chiefly polluted runoff from agriculture and from hydromodification.

title: Agricultural nonpoint source pollution

definition.text: Diffuse pollution of water by nutrients, agrochemicals and sediment washed or carried off farmland.

facts.text: Nitrogen and phosphorus arrive as fertilizer, manure, wastewater or sludge, and also enter runoff from crop residues, irrigation water, wildlife and atmospheric deposition.
Pesticides such as DDT or atrazine travel through waterways or are carried on the wind as spray drift.
Ploughing large tracts exposes and loosens buried soil, so storms erode it more easily and carry more fertilizer and pesticide into nearby water.
Controls include contour ploughing, mulching, crop rotation, perennial crops, riparian buffers, conservation tillage, nutrient management plans and integrated pest management.

notes: Draws on both 'Agricultural operations' sections of the page (Principal sources and Control).

definition.text: Disease-causing bacteria and viruses carried in polluted runoff, a danger chiefly when they reach public drinking water.

facts.text: They include Cryptosporidium parvum, Giardia lamblia, Salmonella, norovirus and other viruses, and parasitic worms.
Coliform bacteria in runoff are a common indicator of water pollution but do not themselves cause disease.
Sources include poorly managed livestock, faulty septic systems, pet waste, over-application of sewage sludge and sewer overflows.

title: Heavy metals in soil

definition.text: Metals such as lead, mercury, zinc and cadmium that resist breakdown and are among the commonest soil contaminants.

facts.text: They come from sewage sludge, mining, vehicle emissions, fossil fuel combustion, urban runoff, industry and landfills, and from some fertilizers made from mined materials.
Heavy metals and metalloids contaminate 19% of China's agricultural soils, and some 12 million tonnes of its grain are contaminated by heavy metals each year.
Within 1.1 km of the Sudbury nickel-copper smelter in Canada, soil held up to 5,104 ppm nickel and 2,892 ppm copper, and nearby plants contained nickel, copper and aluminium.
Some metals are more soluble in oxidizing conditions and others more mobile in reducing ones, so changing soil redox during cleanup can mobilize them.
They easily sorb onto colloids suspended in water, and as ions they can be precipitated into the solid phase.
Unlike organic pollutants they cannot be degraded; microbes can at best immobilize them, as when mobile U(VI) is reduced to less mobile U(IV), an approach still more conceptual than practical.
Some, such as iron, cobalt, copper and zinc, are essential nutrients that turn toxic in larger amounts; others, such as arsenic, cadmium, mercury and lead, are highly poisonous.
The term has no agreed definition: criteria based on density, atomic number or chemistry cover up to 96 elements, and IUPAC calls the term meaningless and misleading.

contested_note: The term itself is disputed: IUPAC and many reviews reject it, yet it remains widely used in science.

title: Nutrient pollution

definition.text: Water pollution caused by too many nutrients, usually nitrogen or phosphorus, entering water bodies.

facts.text: It is a primary cause of eutrophication of lakes, rivers and coastal waters, where the excess nitrogen or phosphorus stimulates algal growth.
Sources include runoff from farms, septic tank waste, feedlots, emissions from burning fuels, and raw sewage dumped into water.
Nitrogen and phosphorus from fertilizers that crops do not fully use are lost from the fields and degrade air and downstream water quality.
Phosphorus reaches water mostly through soil erosion, since many of its forms adsorb onto soil particles; nitrate travels mainly in water moving through the soil, such as interflow and tile drainage.
Excess nitrogen also drives harmful algal blooms, hypoxia, acid rain, nitrogen saturation in forests and climate change.
Health effects include excess nitrate in drinking water (blue baby syndrome), disinfection by-products, and rashes and breathing problems from swimming in algal blooms.
It costs money through higher water treatment bills, losses to commercial fishing, shellfish and recreational fishing, and reduced tourism income.
Remedies include vegetated buffer zones, constructed wetlands and vegetated ditches on farms, better wastewater treatment, and permits based on the polluter pays principle.

title: Eutrophication

definition.text: The build-up of nutrients in a body of water, boosting the growth of algae and other organisms that may then use up its oxygen.

facts.text: It can be natural, a slow build-up of sediment and nutrients over geological time, or cultural, when sewage, industrial wastewater and fertilizer runoff release nutrients.
Phosphorus usually limits plant growth in fresh water and nitrogen in the sea, so excess phosphorus fuels eutrophication of lakes and excess nitrogen that of marine waters.
Algal blooms shade out bottom-dwelling plants; when the algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up oxygen, and the anoxia kills fish and invertebrates.
Severe blooms, called red tides, release toxins as they die and can leave dead zones with no life, sharply reducing biodiversity.
Each summer hypoxic bottom water forms where the Mississippi River enters the Gulf of Mexico, a dead zone comparable in area to New Jersey.
The problem grew with chemical fertilizers in the mid-1900s green revolution; since phosphate detergents were phased out in the 1970s, sewage and agriculture dominate phosphate inputs.
Prevention means cutting nutrients from sewage, agriculture and other sources; shellfish and seaweed can also take up nitrogen and so curb cyanobacterial blooms.

definition.text: A market-based form of water quality trading in which polluters exchange credits for reducing nutrient pollution.

facts.text: It works because sources in one watershed can face very different costs to control the same pollutant, so those with cheap controls sell reduction credits to those with costly ones.
Its principle is 'polluter pays', usually tied to a regulatory requirement to take part.
A 2013 review found three kinds of funders, beneficiaries, polluters and public good payers, with governments and NGOs initiating most payments.

definition.text: Estimating how much of the nutrient load reaching a water body comes from each sector, after attenuation or treatment.

facts.text: In Europe agriculture is typically the main source of nitrogen in water bodies, while in many countries households and industry contribute most of the phosphorus.
Load-oriented models apportion sources from in-stream monitoring data; source-oriented models calculate diffuse emissions from export coefficients of similar catchments.
Ireland's Source Load Apportionment Model estimates nitrogen and phosphorus sources without in-stream data by combining point discharges, diffuse land-use sources and catchment hydrogeology.

title: Bioremediation

definition.text: Using organisms, living or dead, typically bacteria, microalgae, fungi or plants, to remove pollutants from soil, water, air and other media.

facts.text: It exploits organisms' natural ability to absorb, accumulate and degrade pollutants, and aims to be more sustainable, cheaper and more scalable than physicochemical treatment.
Most bioremediation is inadvertent, by native organisms; research focuses on speeding it up by inoculating sites with organisms or supplying nutrients.
It typically works by oxidation, which makes organic compounds more water-soluble and degradable; in the end biodegradation turns hydrocarbons into carbon dioxide and water.

Most processes are redox reactions: an added electron acceptor, usually oxygen, oxidizes pollutants such as hydrocarbons, or an electron donor reduces nitrate, perchlorate, chlorinated solvents and similar pollutants.
Organic pollutants can be biodegraded, but heavy metals cannot, only oxidized or reduced, so bioremediation offers few solutions for them.

Techniques are in situ, treating the site directly, or ex situ, treating excavated material; they include bioventing, bioattenuation, biosparging, biopiles, windrows, landfarming and phytoremediation.
Its main challenge is rate: the processes are slow.
After the 2010 Gulf of Mexico oil spill, bacteria and archaea able to use petroleum as a source of carbon and energy were used to restore the coast.

notes: S:c47bd3861d26 (lead) calls adding specialized microbial cultures 'biostimulation'; S:2d603ff7f641 calls the same step bioaugmentation, which matches the Bioaugmentation and Biostimulation pages. Source slip, not used.

definition.text: Raising the flow of air or oxygen into the unsaturated zone of soil to speed the natural in situ breakdown of hydrocarbon contaminants.

facts.text: It is the commonest aerobic bioremediation, supplying oxygen as the electron acceptor to oxidize petroleum, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, phenols and other reduced pollutants.
Microbes readily degrade components of gasoline, kerosene, diesel and jet fuel under aerobic conditions, but resistance to biodegradation rises with molecular weight.
It is an inexpensive treatment, but decontaminating a site can take a few years.
Below the water table, oxygen comes from recirculated aerated water, pure oxygen, peroxides or air sparging; water in equilibrium with air holds only 8 to 10 mg/L of oxygen.

definition.text: Groundwater remediation by injecting oxygen, and possibly nutrients, into saturated contaminated zones so that indigenous bacteria degrade pollutants faster.

facts.text: Where bioventing aerates the unsaturated zone, biosparging targets the saturated zone below the water table.
In air sparging, air is injected below the water table at a pressure high enough to overcome the water's hydrostatic pressure and the soil's resistance to air flow.

title: Natural attenuation

definition.text: The natural breakdown of contaminants by a site's own microbes, with no human intervention, though the site must still be monitored.

facts.text: It works through dilution, evaporation, sorption onto soil or plant particles and biodegradation, but only once the source is removed and little contamination remains.
Agencies check contaminant levels in soil and water over time, so it is often called monitored natural attenuation, typically used after more active in situ treatment.
Natural recovery is one of the broad categories of bioremediation, beside biostimulation and bioaugmentation.
Monitored natural attenuation is among the techniques for remediating derelict soils, along with leaching, air sparging, soil conditioners, phytoremediation and bioremediation.
Contaminants can also become less bioavailable with time, while microbes and ecosystems adapt to them.
Injecting oxygen to speed aerobic attenuation can suppress anaerobic attenuation where reducing conditions favour anaerobic bacteria.

notes: S:70f10696f089 says bioattenuation happens 'with the addition of nutrients or bacteria', contradicting S:96f207efe6ae (no human involvement); 'without' was probably meant. Not used.

definition.text: Ex situ treatments in which excavated soil is heaped and aerated, by pumps in biopiles or by regular turning in windrows, to speed microbial breakdown of pollutants.

facts.text: Biopiles, like bioventing, remove petroleum pollutants by boosting aerobic degradation; their aeration systems push air in under positive pressure or draw it out under negative pressure.
Windrows work like composting: periodic turning aerates the soil and spreads contaminants evenly, which speeds bioremediation.
Ex situ methods usually cost more than in situ ones because of excavation and transport to a treatment facility.

definition.text: Bioremediation without oxygen, in which an added electron donor drives the reduction of oxidized pollutants such as chlorinated solvents, explosives and nitrate.

facts.text: Added organic substrates are first fermented to hydrogen and volatile fatty acids such as acetate and lactate, which supply carbon and energy to bacteria.
Substrates go in through wells, by direct push, or in trenches such as permeable reactive barriers or biowalls; slow-release edible oils stay in place longer.
Reductive dehalogenation of TCE can stall at DCE and vinyl chloride, suspected or known carcinogens, but Dehalococcoides can reduce them further to harmless ethene.

definition.text: Using microbes to break down pesticide residues in contaminated soil, seen as more promising than other ways of dealing with pesticide contamination.

facts.text: Many sites worldwide are contaminated with agrochemicals, which often resist biodegradation by design.
Lindane, a common 20th-century insecticide still produced today, reduces beneficial soil bacteria such as nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.
Grouped strains of Actinobacteria degrade pesticides more efficiently, but they have only been used in the laboratory, and their cost and scalability are unproven.

definition.text: The drawbacks that keep bioremediation rarely used: slow rates, pollutants that cannot biodegrade, and highly specific microbial needs.

facts.text: Heavy metals and radionuclides do not biodegrade, though they can sometimes be immobilized.
Microbes may not fully mineralize a pollutant and can leave a more toxic compound.
It often takes longer than landfilling or incineration, and small test results are hard to scale up to field operations.
It needs plentiful microbes able to degrade the pollutant in time, preferably indigenous rather than invasive species, and its specific processes require control of many environmental factors.

definition.text: The use of genetic engineering to design organisms for bioremediation, still at the stage of preliminary research.

facts.text: Inserted genes are degradative, coding proteins that break pollutants down, or reporters that monitor pollution, as in Pseudomonas strains given the lux gene to detect naphthalene.
Modified organisms have been made to treat oil spills and break down certain plastics such as PET.
Release raises fears of horizontal gene transfer, so organisms can be built to survive only under set conditions and tagged with bioluminescence genes for tracking.

title: Bioaugmentation

definition.text: A type of bioremediation that adds specialized microbial cultures to boost the breakdown of pollutants.

facts.text: It is common in municipal wastewater treatment to restart activated-sludge bioreactors, but elsewhere remains more aspirational than practical at scale.
For soils it has been proposed against chlorocarbons from dry cleaners and hydrocarbons from petrol stations, usually with an added electron donor (biostimulation) to favour dechlorinating microbes.
Failures come from the wrong organism, predation, competition with native bacteria and too-small doses; many trials weighed only a strain's degrading ability, not its fitness among existing microbes.

notes: Bioaugmentation page crawled but out of scope and unassigned; drafted because three in-scope pages name it (Soil contamination § Cleanup options, Bioremediation, Biostimulation).

definition.text: A form of bioremediation that uses fungi to decontaminate the environment.

facts.text: Fungi are a cheap, effective and environmentally sound way to remove heavy metals, organic pollutants, dyes, petroleum fuels, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pharmaceuticals, pesticides and herbicides.
Their non-specific enzymes break down substances that bacteria degrade poorly, such as pharmaceuticals like paracetamol, and fragrances.
It needs no expensive equipment, so it suits small-scale uses such as mycofiltration of household wastewater and filtering industrial effluent.
In creosote-soaked soils rich in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, mycoremediation has proven the most successful way to stop their spread.
Its by-products can be valuable, such as enzymes like laccase or edible and medicinal mushrooms.
Cold-tolerant Antarctic fungi degrade petroleum compounds where removing contaminated soil would be costly, and acid- and radiation-resistant species may help treat radioactive waste.
In burnt forests, pellets of agarose-coated fungal spores can break down toxins and stimulate regrowth.

definition.text: The capture of metals by fungi, which bind them on their cell surfaces and concentrate them in their fruiting bodies for later removal.

facts.text: Pleurotus, Aspergillus and Trichoderma remove lead, cadmium, nickel, chromium, mercury, arsenic, copper, boron, iron and zinc on land and in water.
Metals enter the mycelium passively, with little uptake into cells; strains from long-polluted sites tolerate them best, and diluting the water greatly improves biosorption.
Metal uptake makes some mushrooms bioindicators: the edible shaggy ink cap signals mercury well, but can then be toxic to eat.
Mycofiltration has recovered 80% of the gold from electronic waste, and dead fungal cell walls can filter heavy metals and radionuclides out of industrial effluents.

definition.text: The breakdown of organic pollutants by fungi, especially white rot fungi, using the enzymes and acids they secrete to digest lignin and cellulose.

facts.text: Lignin and cellulose are long-chain carbon compounds much like many organic pollutants; the ligninolytic enzymes include lignin peroxidase, manganese peroxidase, laccase and cytochrome P450.
Fungi degrade petroleum fuels, phenols, PCBs in soil (Pleurotus ostreatus) and polyurethane, though they may sometimes only pave the way for later microbial activity.
White rot fungi degrade pesticides such as endosulfan, chlorpyrifos and atrazine in clay-loam soils, and dyes including the carcinogenic Congo red.
Pentachlorophenol, a wood preservative ranked among the worst environmental pollutants, has been intensively studied for microbial degradation.

definition.text: The removal of soil contaminants by mycorrhizal fungi, used to strengthen phytoremediation.

facts.text: Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi relieve plants' pollutant stress so they grow more biomass, and supply nutrients, especially phosphorus.
The fungi produce proteins that bind heavy metals, lowering their bioavailability.
Fast-spreading mycelium extends the root zone's reach (the hyphosphere), giving plants access to more nutrients and contaminants and boosting helpful bacteria.
Pairings such as Rhizophagus intraradices with Robinia trees or vetiver grass have removed lead, and mycorrhizal reeds have degraded benzene and MTBE from wetland groundwater.

title: Phytoremediation

definition.text: Using living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants; a type of bioremediation.

facts.text: It is proposed as a sustainable alternative to conventional remediation but has never been used at large scale; microbial bioremediation has so far been more successful.
Its main mechanisms are phytoextraction, phytostabilization, phytovolatilization and phytofiltration, along with breakdown of pollutants by plants and by root-zone microbes.
Poplars draw water up through their roots and out through the plant, slowing the downward movement of soluble contaminants towards groundwater: biological hydraulic containment.
Salt-tolerant halophytes can extract salt from saline soil (phytodesalination), and growing them reduces sodium carbonate in alkali soils.
Breeding and genetic engineering can improve plants: tobacco given a bacterial nitroreductase gene removed TNT faster and resisted its toxicity.
Plant growth-promoting bacteria in the rhizosphere speed the movement of heavy metals into hyperaccumulator roots by producing chelating or solubilizing agents.
Natural compounds such as exogenous polyamines let plants tolerate higher pollutant levels and take up more of them.

notes: S:cdf6e72d82d1 (microbial bioremediation more successful) carries a CITATION NEEDED tag.

title: Phytoextraction

definition.text: Using plants whose roots absorb contaminants from soil or water and concentrate them in harvestable above-ground biomass.

facts.text: Hyperaccumulators take up very high amounts; the arsenic-accumulating Chinese brake fern has been proposed for stripping arsenic from contaminated soil.
Fast-growing non-accumulators such as poplars and willows take up little per plant but could still remove a considerable amount of contaminant.
Heavy metals are often too immobile for plants to absorb, so assisted phytoextraction adds a chelator to make them more soluble.
Metal-hyperaccumulating metallophytes underpin phytomining, a proposed way to collect valuable metals without excavation.

notes: Bioremediation § Heavy metals (S:3ef706075fec) calls metal extraction by hyperaccumulating plants impractical so far; consistent with Phytoremediation never having been used at scale.

definition.text: Using plants to contain pollutants for the long term by lowering their mobility in soil, holding them near the roots rather than in plant tissue.

facts.text: It reduces erosion, runoff and leaching and lowers the contaminant's bioavailability.
Vegetative caps have been used to stabilize and contain mine tailings.
Root mats of meadow grasses may immobilize radioactive materials; some soil amendments reduce their mobility at one concentration but increase it at another.

definition.text: The use of plants to degrade organic pollutants, also called phytotransformation.

facts.text: It has been proposed for herbicides, trichloroethylene and methyl tert-butyl ether, and a pathway for plant transformation of TNT has been proposed.
Plants have been called a 'green liver' because they handle foreign compounds much as the human liver does.

definition.text: Boosting soil microbes' breakdown of organic contaminants in the rhizosphere, the soil around roots; also called rhizodegradation.

facts.text: Roots release carbohydrates and acids that stimulate microbes, which then biodegrade the contaminants.
Plant litter and organic matter help keep soil microbial diversity from being lost to contaminants.
It has been tested with petroleum, PCBs and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.

definition.text: Removing substances from soil or water through plants that turn them into more volatile, often less polluting forms and release them into the air.

facts.text: Selenium can leave soil this way as dimethyl selenide, and mercury as the element.
Poplars, with their high transpiration rates, have been promoted for removing volatile organic compounds.

title: Rhizofiltration

definition.text: Phytoremediation that filters contaminated groundwater, surface water or wastewater through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients.

facts.text: Like phytoextraction it traps contaminants, mainly heavy metals, in harvestable biomass, but it treats water while phytoextraction treats soil.
Plants are usually raised in a greenhouse first, then planted at the site or fed contaminated water brought to them off site.
In one study sunflower roots cut uranium levels by nearly 95% in 24 hours; removing radionuclides with sunflowers was estimated at $2 to $6 per thousand gallons treated.
Contaminants below rooting depth are missed, reaching regulatory levels can take years, and harvested plants threaten health unless non-fodder crops are used.

notes: Rhizofiltration page is crawled but out of scope; used as the concept's own article. Also cites Phytoremediation § Rhizofiltration (S:fd868cf11d25).

definition.text: Using plants as biosensors of subsurface contamination, to map contaminant plumes from what they take up.

facts.text: Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene turn up in tree trunks at concentrations related to those in groundwater.
Standard methods take a core from the trunk, often with an increment borer, for laboratory analysis.
It could streamline site investigations and lower cleanup costs, but has not yet been put to practical use.

definition.text: A physical, in situ treatment that removes volatile contaminants from unsaturated (vadose zone) soil by drawing them out as gas.

facts.text: Vacuum blowers and extraction wells pull gas through the ground, moving contaminants from sorbed, dissolved and pure phases into the gas, which is treated above ground.
It is in essence the vadose-zone counterpart of pump-and-treat for groundwater.
It suits contaminants with high Henry's law constants, such as many chlorinated solvents and hydrocarbons, and the US EPA treats it as a mature presumptive remedy.
It uses standard wells and off-the-shelf equipment, disturbs the site little, and can treat large soil volumes at reasonable cost.
Volatile trichloroethene in permeable, low-carbon sand is readily removed, but naphthalene held in clay layers needs longer treatment or enhancements.
Zones of low air flow, high moisture or strong adsorption cause tailing and rebound, and extraction rates typically fall over time.
Enhancements include directional drilling and fracturing to improve gas flow, and hot air or steam injection to raise volatility and dry the soil.
In air sparging, air injected into groundwater is collected through SVE wells; passive SVE driven by barometric pumping can enhance monitored natural attenuation.

title: SVE off-gas treatment

definition.text: Treating the contaminated vapour drawn out by soil vapor extraction before release, most often by thermal oxidation or activated carbon adsorption.

facts.text: Other options include biofiltration, non-thermal plasma, photocatalytic destruction, membrane separation and condensation; the choice depends on contaminant, offgas concentration, throughput and cost.
Granular activated carbon suits streams below 500 ppmV, oxidation those up to 4,000 ppmV, and vapour condensation those above 4,000 ppmV.
Thermal oxidizers run at 730 to 820 °C, while catalytic oxidizers use a catalyst to work at 316 to 427 °C.
Activated carbon must be replaced as it saturates and does not remove heavy metals; incineration is controversial because of the risk of releasing dioxins.

notes: Facts 2-4 cite Environmental remediation § Soil vapor extraction (crawled, out of scope).

title: Electrokinetic remediation

definition.text: Using direct electric current passed through the ground to draw organic, inorganic and heavy-metal contaminants out of soil.

facts.text: A site has a direct-current source and anode and cathode electrodes in reservoir wells, placed to fit the contaminant plume; injected electrolyte conducts the current and carries contaminants away.
Two migrations drive it: electromigration (electrophoresis) of charged particles, the dominant one, and electro-osmotic flow of pore fluid running the opposite way.
Contaminants must be dissolved into ionic form to migrate; the low pH that develops keeps metals off soil particle surfaces and releases sorbed heavy metals.
Heavy metals such as cadmium, chromium, mercury, zinc, lead and copper are its main targets; it also treats phenols, nitrates, cyanide, petroleum hydrocarbons and radioactive contamination.
At 20 to 30 volts, alkali metals moved 50 to 60 cm per day per volt but heavy metals only 10 to 20, perhaps because heavy metals desorb and dissolve slowly.

It works in situ in saturated or unsaturated low-permeability soils, removing up to 90% of heavy metals from kaolinite and clayey sands; highly permeable soils, counterintuitively, lower its efficiency.
Undissolvable contaminants stay put, long runs acidify soil near the electrodes, buried metal objects short-circuit the system, and polarization lowers its electric potential.
The Lasagna Process, developed at Paducah, Kentucky, in 1995, builds horizontal treatment layers through the soil and removed 98% of trichloroethylene in its first test.

notes: Apparent slips for verification: S:b243c82e072b calls both clay (up to 90% removal) and peat (about 65%) 'low permeable', after saying highly permeable soils lower efficiency; S:c7e9d5b1e98d names 'chromium (IV)', probably chromium(VI). Neither is used.

definition.text: Using geographic information system software to map and analyse contaminants in soil, water and air.

facts.text: Spatial analysis identifies, monitors and assesses pollutants, drawing on remote sensing, lidar, GeoAI and WebGIS, and flags high-risk metal-contaminated sites needing remediation.
Spatial interpolation makes remediation and monitoring of soil and water contaminants more efficient.
Urban soils gather heavy elements from transport, industry and natural weathering, and some of the most contaminated soils surround mines.
At Idrija, Slovenia, soil absorbed mercury from a mine worked for over 500 years; a GIS model mapped its emission from soil, which peaked in July.

title: DRASTIC aquifer vulnerability index
article: GIS in environmental contamination#DRASTIC Summary Index Score modeled using GIS

definition.text: A score, often mapped with GIS, that rates how prone an aquifer is to contamination under its hydrological conditions.

facts.text: Its seven factors spell DRASTIC: depth to water, net recharge, aquifer media, soil media, topography, impact of the vadose zone and hydraulic conductivity.
Each factor carries a weight from one to five, and a lower index means a lower risk of aquifer contamination.
The score shows authorities which areas are most vulnerable so they can put protective measures in place.

title: Hyperaccumulator

definition.text: A metallophyte plant that grows in metal-rich soil or water, absorbing metals through its roots and storing them in its leaves.

facts.text: It concentrates metals to levels toxic to related species not adapted to metalliferous soils; about 85–90% of hyperaccumulators are obligate metallophytes.
One threshold is over 1000 mg/kg of dry weight for nickel, copper, cobalt, chromium or lead, and over 10,000 mg/kg for zinc or manganese.
About 450 species, including Arabidopsis and other Brassicaceae, take up metals such as arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury and nickel at 100–1000 times the levels in sister species.
Their roots take up metal faster, pass it to shoots more quickly and store large amounts, owing to differing expression and regulation of genes shared with related plants.
Alpine pennycress hyperaccumulates cadmium, lead and zinc, holding up to 380 mg/kg cadmium in its leaves; overexpression of the zinc transporter gene ZNT1 underlies its zinc uptake.
Toxic metal levels in leaves may deter herbivores and pathogens, the 'elemental defense hypothesis'.
Introduced species can invade: nickel-accumulating Alyssum brought to Oregon in the 1990s for phytomining spread into serpentine habitats and was declared a noxious weed in 2009.
They are widely discussed for phytoremediation, but commercial use remains aspirational; sunflowers removed caesium-137 and strontium-90 from a pond after the Chernobyl accident.

notes: The 1000/10,000 mg/kg threshold comes from Phytoremediation § Hyperaccumulators (S:0966ad51b6ca). Practicality is judged differently across pages (S:be211a7ad1bb aspirational; S:49cb8c8e901f field trials support feasibility; S:3ef706075fec impractical), not flagged as a debate.

definition.text: Extracting heavy metals from soil with hyperaccumulating plants, then collecting and refining the metals from the harvested biomass; also called agromining.

facts.text: Rufus Chaney, a USDA agronomist, proposed it in 1983; he and Alan Baker first tested it in 1996.
It could in principle harm the environment less than conventional mining and recover low-grade metals from mine waste.
A 2021 review judged its commercial viability limited because it is slow and inefficient; by mid-2024 one nickel project had extracted less than a kilo of usable nickel.
In 2025 a start-up raised 45 million dollars to commercialize nickel phytomining from mine tailings.

definition.text: A plant able to survive in metal-rich soil, classed as a metal indicator, excluder or hyperaccumulator.

facts.text: Obligate metallophytes survive only where heavy metals are present; facultative ones tolerate them but are not confined to such soils.
Metal excluders absorb metals only at their roots.
Metal indicators accumulate heavy metals in shoots and leaves but eventually succumb to their toxicity.

title: Landfarming

definition.text: An ex situ treatment in which contaminated soil, sediment or sludge is mixed into the surface soil and periodically tilled so that microbes degrade the contaminants.

facts.text: It has long been used for drill cuttings, oily sludge and other petroleum refinery wastes, with ordinary farm equipment.
A clay or composite liner commonly intercepts leaching contaminants to protect groundwater, though one is not always required.
PAHs with more rings, and more chlorinated or nitrated compounds, degrade more slowly; creosote, pentachlorophenol and bunker C oil are not readily degraded.
Largely uncontrolled conditions slow degradation, inorganic contaminants are not degraded, hydrocarbon levels above 7% poison the microbes, and microbes turn hydrocarbons into greenhouse gases.

notes: S:df1644941bf3 (creosote, PCP, bunker C oil) carries a CITATION NEEDED tag. Bioremediation § Landfarming adds that contamination deeper than 5 feet must be excavated (S:2c399b7573c8).

title: In situ thermal desorption

definition.text: A soil remediation technology that heats contaminated soil in place, sometimes under vacuum, to drive off or destroy pollutants; also called thermal conduction heating.

facts.text: Soil heated up to 900 °C releases pollutants by vaporization, steam distillation, oxidation or pyrolysis, and a vacuum system captures them.
Electric or gas-fired thermal wells set in arrays heat the soil by conduction, and vapour extraction wells collect the contaminants.
It works in tight soils such as clay, above and below the water table, at temperatures from under 100 °C to above the boiling point of water.
Shell Oil developed it in the late 1980s out of enhanced oil recovery research and commercialized it in the mid-1990s.

notes: S:293cac1262d2 (mid-1990s commercialization) carries a CITATION NEEDED tag.

definition.text: Modifying the environment, chiefly by adding nutrients or electron acceptors or donors, to stimulate bacteria already present that can carry out bioremediation.

facts.text: Additions include phosphorus, nitrogen, oxygen and carbon such as molasses; for halogenated contaminants without oxygen, organic electron donors let native microbes use the contaminants as electron acceptors.
Its main advantage is that native microbes, suited to the subsurface and spread through it, do the work; bioaugmentation can enhance it.
Tight clays make additives hard to spread and fractures channel them, so subsurface investigation and a pilot study should come before full-scale design.
It is used mainly for hydrocarbon and chemical spills, with nitrogen and phosphorus key for marine oil spills, and may also help with herbicides.

title: Surfactant leaching

definition.text: Decontaminating water or soil by mixing it with surfactants and then leaching out the emulsified contaminants.

facts.text: In oil recovery the commonest surfactants are ethoxylated alcohols and nonylphenols, sulphates, sulphonates and biosurfactants.
In surfactant-enhanced aquifer remediation, surfactant solution is pumped from injection wells through contaminated zones to extraction wells to remove non-aqueous phase liquids.

notes: Fact 2 cites Environmental remediation § SEAR (crawled, out of scope).

title: Toxicity characteristic leaching procedure

definition.text: A chemical analysis method that measures how mobile organic and inorganic substances in liquid, solid and mixed wastes are, by leaching them.

facts.text: The sample's pH is set, then it is leached with an acetic acid and sodium hydroxide solution at 1:20 sample to solvent and tumbled for 18 hours to mimic long leaching in the ground.
Landfills use the results to decide whether to accept a waste; above the limits it must go to a hazardous waste facility.
Construction soil and spent abrasive are often tested this way for lead.

notes: US regulatory test method under RCRA; excluded as country-specific regulation per the brief. Soil contamination § Causes (S:d378b4a4eb20) uses it for lead in coal ash.

definition.text: Organic compounds that resist chemical, biological and light-driven breakdown, are toxic, and persist in the environment.

facts.text: Most are pesticides or insecticides; others are solvents, pharmaceuticals and industrial chemicals, and only a few arise naturally, as from volcanoes and forest fires.
They are typically halogenated compounds whose carbon–chlorine bonds resist hydrolysis and photolysis, and their high fat solubility lets them bioaccumulate in fatty tissue.
They volatilize from soils, vegetation and water, travel long distances in air and settle again, reaching places where they were never used, such as Antarctica and the Arctic.
They dissolve poorly in water but are easily captured by solid particles and dissolve in oils and fats.
The 2001 Stockholm Convention named a 'dirty dozen', including aldrin, chlordane, dieldrin, DDT, PCBs and dioxins; new POPs such as PFOS have been added since.
Indoor air and dust POP levels often exceed outdoor levels in air and soil.
Efforts focus more on banning their production and use worldwide than on removing them from the environment.

definition.text: An organic compound made of several fused aromatic rings, formed mostly by incomplete burning of organic matter.

facts.text: Sources include engine exhaust, incinerators, forest fires, coal, petroleum, oil spills and creosote; soil near industrial sites such as creosote works can be heavily contaminated.
Two- and three-ring PAHs spread widely dissolved in water or as gases, while heavier ones travel on particles and settle more locally.
They have a strong affinity for organic carbon, so organic-rich sediments are substantial sinks for them.
Across 76 sites in London's urban soils, the 16 parent PAHs ranged from 4 to 67 mg/kg dry soil, averaging 18 mg/kg, dominated by combustion-derived four- to six-ring forms.
Microbial breakdown is the dominant way PAHs are transformed in the environment, and earthworms are claimed to speed it up.
Unlike many persistent pollutants, they do not biomagnify up food chains, because most vertebrates metabolize and excrete them fairly quickly.
Exposure is linked to cancers, and the EU and US EPA regulate PAH concentrations in air, water and soil, with benzo[a]pyrene the usual marker compound.
Burning moorland vegetation adds PAHs to the peat surface.

definition.text: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances: synthetic chemicals with many fluorine atoms on a carbon chain, so stable they are called 'forever chemicals'.

facts.text: Thousands of PFAS have been made since Teflon in 1938, for waterproof fabrics, carpets, food packaging, firefighting foam and cosmetics.
They occur in rainwater, groundwater, wastewater and soil, with the highest levels at wastewater plants and landfills; firefighting foam has contaminated land near airports and air bases.
Soil contamination raises PFAS in foods such as white rice, coffee and animals reared on the land, and crop uptake is one route to human exposure.
Soil PFAS has been found as far away as Antarctica, and a 2024 study found harmful levels in 31% of 45,000 groundwater samples from areas without obvious sources.
Exposure is linked to cancers, thyroid disease, lowered immunity and fertility, and high cholesterol.
PFOS and PFOA were added to the Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants in 2009 and 2019.
On average PFAS concentrations double with each step up a food web, though compounds vary widely.
Treatment options include sorption on activated carbon or biochar, membrane filtration and foam fractionation, or destruction by oxidation, plasma or incineration.

definition.text: Previously developed land, abandoned or underused, that may carry pollution or a risk of it from past industrial use.

facts.text: Examples include abandoned factories, ash ponds, landfills, dry cleaners and petrol stations; typical contaminants are hydrocarbons, solvents, pesticides, asbestos and heavy metals such as lead.
Definitions vary between countries, mainly on whether pollution must be present; the US EPA counts land whose reuse is complicated by actual or potential contamination.
Many sites sit unused for decades because cleanup would cost more than the land is then worth, and unknown buried tanks or drums can raise costs further.
Cleanups use in situ thermal treatment, bioremediation, in situ oxidation, soil vapor extraction, binders to stop leaching, and phytoremediation of metals.
Developers often insist on a full site investigation before cleanup begins, to avoid unexpected contamination and costs.
The term was first used in 1992 at a US congressional hearing; by September 2023 the EPA's brownfields program had readied 134,414 acres for reuse.

definition.text: An in situ treatment zone set across a contaminant plume that removes or breaks down contaminants as groundwater flows through it.

facts.text: It is built by digging a trench across the groundwater flow, filling it with reactive material such as iron, carbon or limestone, and covering it with soil.
Contaminants are immobilized by sorption or precipitation, which may need the medium replaced, or transformed, usually by irreversible redox reactions, into less harmful forms.
Zerovalent iron was the first and remains the main barrier material; others include microbe-stimulating materials, surfactant-modified zeolites and peat moss.
Loss of reactivity rather than of permeability most likely limits barrier life, and longevity estimates range from 10 to 100 years.

definition.text: The unintended presence of radioactive substances on surfaces or within solids, liquids or gases, hazardous because their decay emits ionizing radiation.

facts.text: Sources are natural or man-made: uranium, thorium and their decay products occur naturally in rock and soil, and mining, oil and gas extraction and coal use can concentrate them.
A nuclear weapon blast or reactor breach contaminates nearby air, soil, people, plants and animals with fuel and fission products, as around Chernobyl and Fukushima.
Nuclear fallout from 520 atmospheric nuclear explosions between the 1950s and 1980s spread contamination widely.
Its hazard depends on the contaminants' concentration, the energy and type of radiation, and how close they come to body organs.
Large contaminated areas may be covered with concrete, soil or rock to stop it spreading, and cleanup produces radioactive waste.
After Fukushima, a goal was to strip 80 to 95% of caesium-137 from contaminated soil without destroying its organic content, aiming to bring exposure to 1 mSv a year above background.

definition.text: Pollution from a single identifiable source, such as one factory outfall or smokestack.

facts.text: It has negligible extent, so models can treat it as a mathematical point, which sets it apart from nonpoint and area sources.
Water point sources include factories, power plants, municipal sewage treatment plants and some farms, such as concentrated animal feeding operations.
Point sources can contaminate natural, man-made and groundwater reservoirs, threatening human health.

definition.text: A passive physicochemical process by which certain biomass concentrates and binds contaminants such as heavy metals onto its cell structure.

facts.text: Unlike bioaccumulation, which needs a living, respiring organism, biosorption needs no energy and depends on equilibrium and the sorbent's cell-surface composition.
Because metals are only bound to the cell surface, biosorption is reversible, and in one test dead Bacillus sphaericus cells took up 13–20% more chromium than living ones.
Its performance depends strongly on pH, biomass concentration and interactions between different metal ions.
Cheap wastes such as eggshells, peat, fungi, seaweed and crab shells can remove toxic metal ions from water, and biosorbents cost about a tenth as much as ion-exchange resins.

definition.text: A contaminant liquid that is denser than water and does not dissolve in it, such as a chlorinated solvent.

facts.text: When spilled in quantity, DNAPLs sink below the water table and stop only at impermeable layers such as clay or tight bedrock, which makes them hard to find and clean up.
Examples include chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene, PCBs, some PFAS and pesticides.
A pool of chlorinated-solvent DNAPL keeps dissolving slowly and acts as a long-term source feeding dissolved groundwater plumes.
DNAPL moves along the slope of the underlying impermeable layer and can travel against the groundwater gradient; where removal is impractical, containment may be the only option.

definition.text: A hydrocarbon groundwater contaminant that does not dissolve in water and is less dense than it, so it forms a separate floating phase.

facts.text: Once it infiltrates the ground, an LNAPL stops at the water table because it is buoyant; benzene, toluene and xylene are examples.
Because they float on the water table, LNAPLs are easier and cheaper to locate and remove than DNAPLs.

definition.text: Any harmful effect of a chemical substance on plant growth, physiology or metabolism.

facts.text: Effects range from disrupted photosynthesis, water and nutrient uptake, cell division or germination to growth inhibition and plant death.
Over-applied fertilizer salts, urea and its ammonia, and poorly humified compost can all be phytotoxic.
Herbicides can harm non-target plants through spray drift or contaminated straw or manure spread on soil.
Co, Cu, Fe, Ni and Zn are needed in trace amounts but become toxic past a threshold, while metals such as As, Cd and Pb are toxic at any concentration.

definition.text: A remediation method that injects gas into contaminated ground at a pressure above that of the gases already there, cracking the subsurface.

facts.text: The fractures spread like a spider web, so pumps can draw contaminated water out through the cracks.
Substrates can also be injected through the cracks to speed remediation of soil and groundwater.

definition.text: A measure of the total amount of the mixture of hydrocarbons found in crude oil present at a site.

facts.text: Crude oil holds several hundred such compounds, too many to measure separately when testing for contamination.
TPH is the sum of volatile petroleum hydrocarbons (gasoline-range, C6–C10) and extractable petroleum hydrocarbons; diesel-range organics span C10–C28.
Its constituents include hexane, benzene, toluene, xylenes, naphthalene and fluorene.

definition.text: The migration of volatile chemicals, usually VOCs, from contaminated soil or groundwater into the indoor air of buildings above or nearby.

facts.text: VOCs diffuse through porous soil in the vadose zone to beneath buildings, then enter through foundation cracks by advection and diffusion, driven by the building's stack effect.
Pipes, storm drains and elevator shafts act as preferential pathways into buildings.
Indoor exposure can cause headaches and raise the risk of some cancers, and some vapors pose an explosion hazard.
Mitigation includes sub-slab depressurization with a fan and over-pressurizing the building.

definition.text: An approach to cleaning up contaminated land that weighs a remedy's environmental, economic and social effects and seeks to minimize the footprint of the cleanup itself.

facts.text: Footprint analysis covers five core elements: energy, air and atmosphere, materials and waste, land and ecosystem, and water.
There are estimated to be more than 450,000 brownfield sites in the US alone needing significant reinvestment.
Pump-and-treat and dig-and-haul can sometimes have lasting side effects worse than the contamination they address.
Some newer in situ techniques have cut life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions by 50 to 80 percent compared with traditional methods.

definition.text: A soil and groundwater remediation technique that lowers contaminant concentrations by injecting chemical reductants, or placing them in a plume's path, at the site itself.

facts.text: It is the mirror process of in situ chemical oxidation and can treat organic compounds that resist natural degradation.
Zero-valent metals, above all zero-valent iron, are the main reductants, used for example to clean up trichloroethylene and hexavalent chromium.
On iron surfaces, halocarbons are dechlorinated by direct electron transfer from Fe0, by Fe2+ from corrosion, or by hydrogen from anaerobic corrosion with a catalyst.
It is often installed as a permeable reactive barrier, a trench of zero-valent iron, though nanoscale iron can be injected directly into plumes.

definition.text: The use of microorganisms, working in sequence, to degrade polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) at contaminated sites.

facts.text: PCBs are stable, poorly soluble persistent organic pollutants once used as dielectric fluids and coolants; natural degradation takes 3 to 37 years depending on chlorination.
Anaerobic bacteria first dechlorinate PCBs by using them as electron acceptors; aerobic microbes then break the products down through the biphenyl pathway.
PCBs bind tightly to soil, and higher organic carbon and clay content further lower their availability to microbes.
PCBs are toxic to bacteria above 1000 mg/kg, degradation slows sharply below 50 mg/kg, and it gets harder the more chlorines a molecule carries.

definition.text: An intensive in situ remediation method that passes alternating current through soil and groundwater between buried electrodes, heating them until contaminants evaporate.

facts.text: The soil's resistance to current generates heat until water boils at depth; the steam then strips out volatile contaminants, which a vapor recovery system captures and treats at the surface.
It works best on volatile organic compounds such as perchloroethylene and trichloroethylene; less volatile ones such as diesel need more energy.
Current travels mainly through the thin water film on grains, so ERH works in any soil type and in sedimentary bedrock, but cannot dry the ground out.
Electrodes are typically 15 to 20 feet apart with run times under a year; peat or high organic carbon raises the energy needed by adsorbing VOCs.

definition.text: A remediation technology that heats contaminated soil or other solids so that contaminants volatilize and can be separated, then collected or destroyed.

facts.text: A system has two main parts, the desorber and the offgas treatment system, and it is not incineration.
It was used at 69 US Superfund sites through FY2000 and is regarded as a permanent remedy at competitive cost, unlike stabilization, which leaves contaminants on site.
Common desorbers are indirect- and direct-fired rotary cylinders and heated screws; indirect rotary units reach about 1,000 °F with carbon steel shells.
Removing 500 mg/kg of organics from 20,000 tons of soil yields under 3,000 US gallons of liquid, less than one tank truck.

title: Biodegradation

definition.text: The breakdown of organic matter by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.

facts.text: Almost all compounds biodegrade given time, but elements do not, so heavy metal pollutants never biodegrade.
It runs in three stages: biodeterioration, biofragmentation of polymer bonds, and assimilation of the products into microbial cells.
Aerobic breakdown is faster, while anaerobic breakdown also yields methane and shrinks the mass of material more.
Its rate depends on light, water, oxygen, temperature and the compound's bioavailability, and can be measured by the CO2 microbes release in soil respirometry tests.

notes: Distinct from the organic-matter chapter's Decomposition entry: this page frames breakdown of materials and pollutants, including the point that metals cannot biodegrade.

definition.text: The harnessing of microbes' natural ability to degrade, transform or accumulate pollutants such as oil, PCBs, PAHs, pharmaceuticals, radionuclides and metals.

facts.text: Hydrocarbons and halogenated compounds were long doubted to break down without oxygen, until anaerobic hydrocarbon-degrading and reductively dehalogenating bacteria were isolated.
Bioavailability, the amount of a pollutant physically accessible to microbes, is a key factor in efficient biodegradation.
Most soil clays, kaolinite excepted, slowed bacterial degradation of 2-picoline by adsorbing the substrate.
Hydrocarbon-degrading bacteria remove a considerable share of the petroleum entering marine systems.

title: Acid mine drainage treatment

definition.text: The neutralization of acidic mine outflow and removal of its dissolved metals, using limestone, lime, calcium silicate, ion exchange, wetlands or sulfide precipitation.

facts.text: Crushed limestone is the cheapest neutralizer, but its grains become armored with gypsum and an iron–aluminium hydroxysulfate film that stops calcite from dissolving.
In lime treatment, a lime slurry raises the water to about pH 9, where most toxic metals precipitate and settle out as sludge.
Constructed wetlands are cheap: sediment bacteria reduce sulfate to sulfide, which binds and precipitates heavy metals, though they handle only limited metal loads.
Sulfate-reducing bacteria can also be used in reactors, yielding bicarbonate that neutralizes acidity and hydrogen sulfide that precipitates metals.
