definition.text: The yellow-orange iron(III) hydroxide that precipitates when the pH of acid mine drainage rises above 3.

facts.text: Iron oxides, oxyhydroxides and sulfates such as jarosite can also form; all of them discolor water and smother streambed life.
Precipitation releases more hydrogen ions, lowering pH further, and very rich deposits can be recovered for pigments.

definition.text: The biotic and abiotic byproducts of farming that contaminate or degrade the environment and ecosystems or harm people and their interests.

facts.text: It ranges from point-source discharges to diffuse, landscape-level non-point source pollution and air pollution.
Farm pollutants include sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts, and reach lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater.
Poor practices behind it include badly run animal feeding operations, overgrazing, plowing and excessive or badly timed fertilizer and pesticide use.
Persistent herbicides such as 2,4-D and atrazine can last up to 20 years, and pesticides accumulate in animals that eat contaminated pests and soil organisms.
Plastic sheeting, mulch and storage bags put plastics into soil; a 2021 FAO study estimated 10 million tons of agricultural plastic waste a year.
Manures and biosolids can carry pharmaceuticals and personal care products along with their fertilizer value.

definition.text: The movement of dissolved pesticides through the soil to sites beyond their target, a major source of groundwater pollution.

facts.text: Leaching depends on the soil, the pesticide, and rainfall and irrigation.
It is worst for water-soluble pesticides with weak soil adsorption, on sandy soils, and when heavy watering follows soon after application.
Mixing areas, machinery-washing sites and disposal areas are sources as well as treated fields.

definition.text: A chemical or biological agent used to deter, incapacitate or kill pests, including herbicides, insecticides, nematicides and fungicides.

facts.text: Herbicides are the most common, at about 50% of all pesticide use worldwide.
Agriculture used 3.73 million tonnes of active ingredients in 2023, double the 1990 figure, averaging 2.40 kg per hectare of cropland.
Over 98% of sprayed insecticides and 95% of herbicides end up somewhere other than their target, including air, water and soil.
The Stockholm Convention banned persistent pesticides such as DDT, whose soil half-life of 2–15 years means residues are still detectable in people.
Pesticides must now be degradable; halogens in a molecule slow aerobic breakdown, and adsorption to soil slows movement but also reduces availability to microbial degraders.
Pests can evolve resistance, prompting new products or higher doses that worsen pollution.

definition.text: The transformation of a pesticide into a benign substance compatible with the environment where it was applied.

facts.text: An estimated 1 to 2.5 million tons of active ingredients are used each year, making pesticides an important diffuse chemical input.
Documented soil half-lives are typically days to weeks, yet residues occur everywhere at ng/liter to low μg/liter levels.
Degradation combines biotic transformation by microbes, the largest contributor, with abiotic chemical and photochemical reactions.
Redox gradients in soils, sediments and aquifers often decide which transformations can occur, and photochemistry reaches only submillimeter soil layers.
Microbes that cleave glyphosate's stable C–P bond are widespread, and bacterial enzymes dechlorinate atrazine to hydroxyatrazine in soil.
Pesticides persist for decades in groundwater, perhaps because microbial degradation stalls at low concentrations in nutrient-poor settings.
Rising 13C/12C ratios in a parent compound give direct evidence of degradation, since microbes preferentially transform the lighter isotope.

title: Pesticide transformation products

definition.text: The compounds a pesticide breaks down into, which may keep or even exceed the parent's harmful activity.

facts.text: Being smaller and more polar than their parents, they reach groundwater and surface water more readily.
Europe classes metabolites as nonrelevant, groundwater-relevant (likely above 0.1 μg/liter with parent-like toxicity) or ecotoxicologically relevant.
Tolerating up to 10 μg/liter of nonrelevant metabolites in groundwater is politically contentious: some see no proven health risk, others a breach of the precautionary principle.

contested_note: Whether a 10 μg/liter limit for nonrelevant metabolites in European groundwater is acceptable is disputed.

definition.text: An in situ technique that injects clean air or gas into contaminated saturated soil and groundwater so that volatile organic compounds change from dissolved to vapor form.

facts.text: Pressurized air from wells below the water table forms small bubbles that volatilize contaminants and carry them up into the unsaturated soil.
Vacuum points in the unsaturated zone pull the vapors into a soil vapor extraction system, and the off-gas is treated with granulated activated carbon.
It suits light gasoline constituents such as benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene, but not heavier fuels such as kerosene and diesel.

definition.text: Groundwater pollution, often natural, caused by high concentrations of arsenic in deeper aquifer water.

facts.text: A 2007 study found over 137 million people in more than 70 countries were probably affected by arsenic in drinking water.
The WHO recommends a limit of 10 μg/L, often unattainable in problem areas because arsenic is hard to remove.
Organic matter in aquifer sediments creates anaerobic conditions in which microbes dissolve iron oxides, releasing the arsenic bound to them, so arsenic-rich water is often iron-rich.
It occurs as arsenite and arsenate, soluble forms extracted from the rocks around the aquifer; arsenite is somewhat more acutely toxic.
Millions of tube wells sunk in Bangladesh from the 1970s caused one of the largest mass poisonings; the natural contamination was discovered in 1993.
In the Ganges Delta the affected wells are mostly 20 to 100 meters deep; water below 100 meters meets older sediments already depleted of arsenic.
Irrigating with contaminated water may add significantly to people's dietary arsenic intake.

definition.text: The contamination of groundwater by pollutants released to the ground, or by unwanted natural constituents, that make their way into aquifers.

facts.text: Sources include on-site sanitation, landfill leachate, leaking sewers, petrol stations, fracking and over-applied fertilizer, as well as natural arsenic or fluoride.
A pollutant often forms a plume that spreads through the aquifer and can reach wells, seeps and springs.
Its transport is governed by diffusion, adsorption, precipitation and decay, and analysis considers soil characteristics, site geology and hydrogeology.
Passage through the subsurface can be a reliable natural barrier, but only under favorable conditions; karst limestone and faults offer quick routes for contaminants.
Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene partly decompose in aquifers into other hazards, including dichloroethylene and vinyl chloride.
Nitrate is the most common chemical contaminant of the world's groundwater, and it does not degrade under high-oxygen conditions.
Prevention includes monitoring, land zoning and careful siting of sanitation; once polluted, options are point-of-use treatment, remediation or abandonment.

definition.text: Groundwater contamination that arises naturally from geological processes rather than human activity.

facts.text: Arsenic and fluoride are the most widespread geogenic contaminants; salinity, iron, manganese, uranium, radon and chromium matter more locally.
High fluoride usually reflects fluoride minerals such as fluorite and a lack of calcium in the aquifer; above 1.5 mg/L it can cause dental fluorosis.
WHO tests found 20% of 25,000 Bangladesh boreholes above 50 μg/L arsenic.

definition.text: The die-off and adsorption of pathogens in liquid leaching from pit latrines and septic tanks as it passes through the unsaturated soil to groundwater.

facts.text: Removal depends mostly on travel time to the well; most, but not all, pathogens die within 50 days underground.
It varies with soil type, aquifer type and distance, and long heavy rain can wash the unsaturated zone and open fast pathways.
Biological activity, and so pathogen attenuation, is greatest in the topsoil layers.
A general guideline puts a pit's base at least 2 m above groundwater and 30 m horizontally from a water source.

title: Aquifer vulnerability mapping

definition.text: The mapping of an aquifer's intrinsic vulnerability to pollution by overlaying maps of the physical factors that control it.

facts.text: Shallow unconfined aquifers are most at risk because fewer layers filter out contaminants, and the unsaturated zone can slow or remove pathogens.
The GOD method uses groundwater confinement, overlying strata and depth to groundwater; EPA's DRASTIC uses seven factors including soil media and vadose-zone impact.
Hydrogeologists debate whether vulnerability should be set intrinsically for all contaminants or separately for each pollutant.

contested_note: Hydrogeologists disagree on whether vulnerability should be assessed generally or pollutant by pollutant.

definition.text: The treatment of polluted groundwater by removing pollutants or converting them into harmless products.

facts.text: Between 25 and 40 percent of the world's drinking water comes from boreholes and dug wells.
Wastes long disposed of on land surfaces percolated into groundwater, and fertilizer, pesticides, spills, urban runoff and landfills still pollute it.

Techniques are biological (bioaugmentation, bioventing, biosparging, bioslurping, phytoremediation), chemical (precipitation, ion exchange, oxidation, surfactants) and physical (pump and treat, air sparging, dual-phase extraction).
Most treatments combine several technologies.

definition.text: A technique combining bioventing with vacuum pumping of floating free product (LNAPL) to recover it from groundwater and soil and bioremediate the soil.

facts.text: A slurp tube reaching into the free-product layer draws up liquid and soil gas together, lifting oil off the water table and capillary fringe.
Air drawn into the unsaturated zone drives aerobic biodegradation of the hydrocarbons.

definition.text: A high-vacuum technology, also called multi-phase extraction, that removes both contaminated groundwater and soil vapor through one well.

facts.text: Pumping depresses the water table, exposing the often highly contaminated capillary fringe, whose contaminants are then removed by vapor extraction.
Treating the capillary fringe can shorten cleanup time at a site.

definition.text: The cleanup of hazardous substances by removing, treating or containing contaminants in soil, groundwater, sediment and other environmental media.

facts.text: Remediation may be required before land is redeveloped, and developers may get incentives for voluntary cleanup.
Action is governed by regulation, or by human-health and ecological risk assessment where no standards exist; Europe often uses the Dutch standards.
Excavation can mean simply hauling soil to a regulated landfill, or aerating it to release VOCs.
Barrier walls, built by deep soil mixing, jet grouting, freezing or slurry walls, contain contaminants instead of removing them.

definition.text: A remediation method that pumps contaminated groundwater to the surface and purifies it, typically by passing it through vessels of adsorbent such as activated carbon.

facts.text: It is one of the most widely used groundwater remediation technologies.
It can quickly cut high concentrations, but sorption–desorption equilibrium in the soil makes the low levels required by standards hard to reach.
Being slow and expensive, it is best used to control the hydraulic gradient and stop a release from spreading.

definition.text: A treatment that mixes a binder into contaminated soil to stop or reduce the mobility of contaminants.

facts.text: Stabilization adds reagents that make constituents chemically more stable; solidification locks contaminants in a solid product that air and rain cannot reach.
Its uptake is held back by cheap landfill disposal, doubts about durability and contaminant release, and liability for contaminants left on site.
CO2 emissions from the cement used are a growing obstacle.

definition.text: The use of nano-sized reactive agents to degrade or immobilize contaminants in soil or groundwater.

facts.text: Nanoparticles are injected in situ or used in pump-and-treat, degrading organics by redox reactions or adsorbing and immobilizing metals such as lead or arsenic.
Most field applications have used nano zero-valent iron.
Their high surface area per unit mass makes them fast-reacting, but also makes them clump or react with soil particles, limiting their spread.

definition.text: A form of bioremediation in which insects, such as fly larvae, beetles, ants and termites, decontaminate soils.

facts.text: It relies on hardy saprophytic insect larvae that bioaccumulate toxic heavy metals.
Black soldier fly larvae have reduced polluted substrate dry weight by 49% and accumulate cadmium with a bioaccumulation factor of 5.6.

definition.text: The removal of non-aqueous phase liquids from aquifers by pumping a surfactant solution through the contaminated zone from injection to extraction wells.

facts.text: Surfactants raise the mobility and solubility of contaminants sorbed to the saturated soil or present as DNAPL.
Extracted water is treated above ground and the surfactants, which are non-toxic and biodegradable, are reused.
It is used most often for DNAPLs such as trichloroethylene, and often as a first step before in situ oxidation or bioremediation.

definition.text: Any compound of chromium in the +6 oxidation state, a carcinogenic form produced mainly by industry.

facts.text: It is rare in nature but made on a large scale, since virtually all chromium ore is processed through sodium dichromate.
Inhaled it can cause lung cancer, and in drinking water it has been found to cause cancers of the mouth and small intestine.
At neutral pH chromate enters cells through sulfate channels and is reduced to chromium(III), which binds DNA and causes mutagenic damage.
Practical cleanup of water reduces Cr(VI) to Cr(III), a step activated sludge can also perform.

definition.text: Poisoning by cadmium, a naturally occurring toxic metal met in industry, in plant soils and in tobacco smoke.

facts.text: Some phosphate fertilizers contain up to 100 mg/kg cadmium, which can build up in soil.
Chronic exposure softens and weakens bones and irreversibly damages the kidneys, which can shrink by up to 30 percent.
Daily dietary intake is about 8 to 30 μg in Europe and the US but 59 to 113 μg in parts of Japan, where people ate rice irrigated with contaminated water.
Cadmium in bone has a biological half-life of about 30 years.

definition.text: Harm to plants, animals or people caused by excessive concentrations of metals.

facts.text: Copper, iron, manganese and zinc are essential at low levels but toxic at high exposure; arsenic, cadmium, lead, mercury and thallium have no biological role in animals.
Only soluble metal compounds are toxic, acting as coordination complexes; converting them to insoluble forms or binding them with chelators detoxifies them.
Chromium, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and lead bind strongly to sulfur, attaching to enzymes through thiol groups and blocking their function.
IUPAC calls the term 'heavy metals' meaningless and misleading: not all heavy metals are toxic and some toxic metals are not heavy.
Arsenic poisoning mainly comes from naturally arsenic-rich groundwater, while lead poisoning comes from industrial materials such as leaded gasoline and plumbing.
Minamata's 1956 methylmercury release alerted the world to bioaccumulation.

definition.text: The cleanup of soils contaminated by heavy metals through isolation, immobilization, toxicity reduction, physical separation or extraction.

facts.text: Isolation quarantines soil with caps, membranes or buried barriers, while immobilization alters the soil to hinder metal movement.
Toxicity reduction oxidizes or reduces metal ions chemically or biologically into less toxic or mobile forms.
Extraction uses chemicals, high-temperature volatilization or electrolysis, on or off site; the choice depends on the contaminant and site.

definition.text: The study of how toxic chemicals affect organisms, populations and ecosystems, joining toxicology and ecology.

facts.text: It looks at all biological levels from molecules to ecosystems, unlike environmental toxicology, which centres on effects on organisms, especially human health.
Toxicants move through food webs and accumulate, so top predators are often the worst affected.
Besides killing organisms, sublethal doses can impair movement or feeding and so alter competition and predator–prey relations.
Species-rich communities recover from contaminant disturbance more readily than less diverse ones.
Its findings help predict and prevent pollution damage and show how to restore ecosystem services where damage has occurred.

definition.text: Standardized acute and chronic toxicity tests on terrestrial and aquatic organisms, including earthworms, used to rate a chemical's ecological hazard.

facts.text: LC50 is the concentration that kills 50% of test organisms within the test period, which can last up to 96 hours.
EC50 is the concentration causing an adverse effect in 50% of organisms, and NOEC is the highest dose with no statistically significant effect.
Acute toxicity below 1 part per million places a substance in Class I, 1–10 ppm in Class II and 10–100 ppm in Class III.

definition.text: Pollutants found in environmental monitoring that may harm ecosystems or health and are usually not yet regulated.

facts.text: They include pharmaceuticals, personal care products, industrial byproducts and agricultural chemicals, which often escape detection and treatment and persist.
Agricultural runoff after rain or irrigation carries pesticides and pharmaceuticals from soil into rivers, lakes and groundwater.
Water treatment must not simply move them into sludge, since sludge spread on land is another route into the environment.
Explosives such as TNT are major contaminants of groundwater and soils.

definition.text: Bioremediation carried out at the contaminated site itself, without moving the polluted material.

facts.text: It treats groundwater and soils polluted by hydrocarbons, chlorinated compounds, nitrates and toxic metals, using microbes that are introduced or fed with nutrients.
It is one mechanism of natural attenuation; in accelerated forms nutrients or an electron donor are added to grow a target microbe, or microbes are added (bioaugmentation).
Oxygen supply is often the limiting factor for how fast and how well it works.
Compared with ex situ treatment it costs less and carries less risk of cross-contamination.

definition.text: An accelerated in situ bioremediation method, developed by Richard Raymond, that adds nutrients and electron acceptors to contaminated groundwater.

facts.text: Groundwater is pumped up downstream, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream in a loop.
Oxygen can be supplied through injection wells or galleries, or as ozone, half of which decomposes to oxygen within twenty minutes.

definition.text: The breakdown of petroleum hydrocarbons by native soil microbes that use them for energy and carbon.

facts.text: Up to twenty percent of soil microbial populations can metabolize hydrocarbons, mainly aerobically, to carbon dioxide and water.
Long-chain aliphatics degrade most readily; short-chained, branched and quaternary ones less so.
Aromatic compounds with two or three rings degrade at effective rates, but those with four or more resist and are broken down only by cometabolism.
Porous, carbon-rich biochar traps PAHs and gives microbes good conditions to degrade them.

definition.text: The use of bacteria, plants and fungi to catalyze reactions that decontaminate soil, water and sediment affected by radionuclides.

facts.text: Conventional cleanup by excavation and long-distance transport can have estimated costs exceeding a trillion dollars in the US.
The organisms change radionuclides' solubility, bioavailability and mobility to speed their stabilization.
The commonest natural radionuclides in soils are radium-226, radon-222, thorium-232, uranium-238 and potassium-40.
Some fungi can use ionizing radiation as energy, and oyster mushrooms can bioremediate plutonium-239 and americium-241.

definition.text: The enzymatic reduction of radionuclides by bacteria to lower oxidation states, changing their solubility, mobility and radiotoxicity.

facts.text: Anaerobes use the radioisotope as the terminal electron acceptor, for example reducing soluble uranium(VI) to insoluble uranium(IV).
Sulfate-reducing and metal-reducing bacteria also reduce radionuclides indirectly through the metabolites they excrete.
Siderophores and other bacterial chelators can instead raise radionuclide solubility and bioavailability.

definition.text: The removal of radionuclides from soil by plants that carry them from the roots into their shoots.

facts.text: It leaves soil structure and fertility largely intact and suits large areas of low-level contamination, but needs fast, large biomass production.
It works for caesium-137, strontium-90, technetium-99, plutonium-240 and americium-241, among others.
In the Chernobyl zone, mustard greens removed up to 22% of average caesium activity in one growing season.

title: Geochemical background

definition.text: The natural levels of elements and other substances in soil, water and air, set by processes such as weathering, against which contamination is judged.

facts.text: Typical background levels in soil do not exceed about 100 mg/kg for arsenic, lead and nickel, 2 mg/kg for cadmium, 150 mg/kg for copper and 300 mg/kg for zinc.
Chromium background in soil is under 500 mg/kg, and selenium does not exceed 1 mg/kg.
Establishing baseline or background levels of naturally occurring harmful materials in soil, water, air and food is a stated priority of medical geology.
Remediation emission results are compared with natural background levels in the area as well as with zoning standards.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; the definition joins three sentences that use 'background levels' for natural concentrations.
